items.title: E-means: Outperforming k-means in one-tenth the epochs
items.content:
100,000 datapoints in 200 clusters, two wide Gaussians and three small ones, cut off at a box, on a light uniform background. Lloyd has 1 update against 97 per epoch for e-means.

Across a large range of scales and datasets , e-means reaches a test loss below Lloyd's at 25 epochs, in 1.2 to 3 epochs. Measured end to end, that is a 10–45× wall-clock reduction on GPU against the state-of-the-art Lloyd implementation (Flash-KMeans [2] ), and 8–15× on CPU against Faiss [1] . Speed and quality usually trade against each other in k-means, while e-means achieves both better speed and loss.

Given a fixed dataset of n points X = {x 1 , ..., x n } ⊂ R d and an integer k , the k-means problem is to find k centroids C = (c 1 , ..., c k ) minimizing the mean squared distance between each point and its nearest centroid:

It's a static dataset, unlike codebook learning inside VQ-VAEs, where the distribution to cluster is constantly moving.

The goal of e-means is to provide a modern optimization rule for the k-means problem. We started this project from the following observations:

For e-means, we chose to do mini-batch updates with exponential moving averages [6] , which we found to be most efficient for the k-means problem. Contrary to previous mini-batch approaches, e-means requires no hyperparameter tuning because it automatically sets the batch size and step size with scaling laws (see Automatic hyperparameter tuning with scaling laws ). In addition, e-means improves the initialization and the dead-cluster revival strategy, adds a cosine-scheduled decay rate, and introduces a finalization stage that reduces the training loss for a negligible runtime penalty at the end of training. e-means is highly parallelizable, and comes with specialized kernels that translate its algorithmic advantage into wall-clock speedups.

Each mini-batch updates every cluster's count and sum. The centroid is their ratio.

Everything is derived from scaling laws.

Novel initialization and finalization methods. The run ends on each cluster's exact last-epoch mean.

The step α anneals from α 0 to 0.1 α 0 , as a learning rate does.

Clusters with size below a threshold are revived by splitting a large cluster.

GPU kernels fuse the nearest-centroid assignment, turning the epoch savings above into matching wall-clock speedups.

The centroid update rule is the central component of e-means. This section aims to provide an overview of update rules for k-means clustering. All methods maintain, for each cluster j , a sum S j and a count N j of the points assigned to it, and take the centroid as their ratio:

They differ only in how S j and N j are updated. Below, s j and n j denote the sum and the count of the points in the current batch that are assigned to cluster j (both zero if none are).

Lloyd’s algorithm [7] assigns every point to its nearest centroid and recomputes the statistics from scratch, using the full dataset as the batch:

so c j is the exact mean of the points currently assigned to it. Each update costs one full pass over the data, and the procedure is repeated a fixed number of times (typically 20 to 50 iterations).

MacQueen’s update [3] accumulates the statistics without ever discarding them:

so c j is the uniform mean of every point assigned to cluster j since the start of training, including points assigned under earlier, possibly poor, centroid positions. This was later partially addressed by Staleness-Reduction Mini-Batch K-Means [8] , a hybrid method between k-means and MacQueen. They obtained important speedups, but only on very low numbers of clusters.

e-means works on mini-batches and replaces this sum with an exponential moving average:

so older assignments are forgotten at rate α , and the centroid tracks recent assignments rather than the whole history. This update rule is typically used for moving distributions, hence their adoption for training VQ-VAEs [6] . What we found is that it’s also extremely efficient for static datasets if…
items.title_ko: 동일한 손실에서 10배 이상 빠른 k-means, e-means
items.summary_ko: e-means는 k-means 문제를 위한 최적화 규칙으로, 여러 규모와 데이터셋에서 25 에폭 동안 학습한 Lloyd 방식보다 낮은 테스트 손실에 1.2~3 에폭 만에 도달했다. 실제 실행 시간 기준으로 GPU에서는 최신 Lloyd 구현인 Flash-KMeans 대비 10~45배, CPU에서는 Faiss 대비 8~15배 빨라졌다고 보고했다. 일반적으로 k-means는 속도와 품질이 상충하지만, e-means는 속도와 손실 모두에서 개선을 보였다고 밝혔다.
items.content_ko: 본문은 10만 개의 데이터 포인트를 200개 클러스터로 나눈 예시로 시작한다. 이 데이터는 넓은 가우시안 분포 두 개와 작은 분포 세 개로 구성되며, 상자 영역으로 잘리고 밝은 균일 배경을 가진다. 에폭당 업데이트 횟수는 Lloyd가 1회, e-means가 97회다. 저자들은 다양한 규모와 데이터셋에서 e-means가 25 에폭 기준 Lloyd보다 낮은 테스트 손실에 1.2~3 에폭 만에 도달했다고 설명한다. 실행 시간을 측정한 결과 GPU에서는 Flash-KMeans [2] 대비 10~45배, CPU에서는 Faiss [1] 대비 8~15배 단축되었다. 본문은 k-means 문제를 정의하고, 정적 데이터셋을 다루는 이 연구가 분포가 계속 변하는 VQ-VAE 내부 코드북 학습과 다르다고 짚는다. e-means는 지수 이동 평균[6]을 활용한 미니배치 업데이트를 사용한다. 본문이 중간에 잘려 있다.

items.title: What's new in Node.js 27
items.content:
New Iterator superpower: zip, zipKeyed, join, and includes Pairing sequences lazily with Iterator.zip()

Combining endless iterators: solar generation and household consumption

Turning columns into objects with Iterator.zipKeyed()

Finishing pipelines with Iterator.prototype.join() and includes()

More accurate sums with Math.sumPrecise()

node:net/promises and async-iterable TCP servers

Virtual File System (node:vfs) is now unflagged

More Node.js Core upgrades: fs, Permissions, Test Runner, and HTTP Atomic temporary files with fs.mkstemp() and native fs.glob()

Built-in Test Runner: stable watch mode and Jest-style mock helpers

Why remove the prototype from req.headers?

Under the hood: V8 15.6, the 4 GB Heap Default, and OpenSSL 4.1

Heads-up: Node.js 27 breaking changes 1. req.headers has a null prototype

2. Memory limits for multi-process deployments

3. V8 serialization format and larger heap snapshots

4. V8 behavior changes that can break tests and caches

5. Deprecations, removals, and platform changes

Frequently Asked Questions Why did Node.js 27 start with an Alpha release in October 2026?

Will Node.js 27 become an LTS release even though 27 is an odd number?

What are the biggest JavaScript features in Node.js 27?

How did the default memory limit change in Node.js 27?

On October 29, 2026, the Node.js team published v27.0.0-alpha.0.0.0 . If you have been using Node.js for a few years, that version string alone probably made you do a double take. Where is the usual October v27.0.0 Current release?

Node.js 27 is the first release to follow the new annual schedule. Under the old schedule, October brought a major release that reached end of life six months later without entering Long Term Support (LTS). October now starts a six-month Alpha phase, ahead of the 27.0.0 Current release in April 2027 and LTS promotion in October 2027.

In this first Alpha, V8 moves from 14.6 to 15.6, adding Iterator.zip() , Iterator.zipKeyed() , Iterator.prototype.join() , Iterator.prototype.includes() , and Math.sumPrecise() . There is a promises API for node:net , along with async-iterable TCP servers. The Virtual File System ( node:vfs ) is now unflagged, the Permission Model gains --allow-env , and HTTP and memory defaults change too.

We’ll start with the JavaScript and Node.js APIs you can use in everyday code, comparing them with the older approaches. Then we’ll cover runtime changes and what to check before upgrading.

The main additions in Node.js 27 so far:

New Iterator helpers ( zip , zipKeyed , join , includes ) pair sequences, join their values into strings, and search them without collecting intermediate arrays.

Math.sumPrecise() sums an iterable of numbers without rounding each intermediate addition.

node:net/promises and async-iterable net.Server let you use async / await to set up TCP servers and sockets.

Virtual File System ( node:vfs ) is unflagged, making in-memory file systems and --vfs-load available without --experimental-vfs .

Core upgrades across fs , permissions, test runner, and http , including atomic temp files with fs.mkstemp() , --allow-env , Jest-style mock helpers, and a 65-second HTTP keepAliveTimeout .

V8 15.6 and OpenSSL 4.1 update sorting and cryptography, and the default heap limit rises to 4 GB on an 8 GB machine.

items.title_ko: Node.js 27의 주요 변경 사항
items.summary_ko: Node.js 27은 Iterator.zip, zipKeyed, join, includes와 Math.sumPrecise를 추가하며, node:net/promises, 가상 파일 시스템 node:vfs의 플래그 해제, 임시 파일용 fs.mkstemp와 네이티브 fs.glob 등을 포함한다. 주의할 점으로 req.headers가 null 프로토타입을 갖게 되는 호환성 변경과, V8 15.6, 기본 힙 4GB, OpenSSL 4.1 업그레이드가 있다.
items.content_ko: Node.js 27은 여러 새 기능을 소개한다. Iterator.zip()은 시퀀스를 지연 방식으로 짝지으며, zipKeyed()는 열을 객체로 바꾼다. Iterator.prototype.join()과 includes()로 파이프라인을 마무리할 수 있다. Math.sumPrecise()는 더 정확한 합계를 제공한다. node:net/promises와 비동기 반복 가능한 TCP 서버도 추가되었다. 가상 파일 시스템 node:vfs는 플래그 없이 사용할 수 있게 되었다. fs.mkstemp()로 임시 파일을 만들고 네이티브 fs.glob도 쓸 수 있다. 테스트 러너는 안정적인 watch 모드와 Jest 스타일 mock 도우미를 제공한다. 호환성 측면에서는 req.headers에 프로토타입이 없어지며, 다중 프로세스 배포의 메모리 제한, V8 직렬화 형식과 큰 힙 스냅샷, V8 동작 변경, 기타 deprecated 항목 등이 있다. 기반 구성요소는 V8 15.6, 기본 힙 4GB, OpenSSL 4.1이다. FAQ에 따르면 Node.js 27은 2026년 10월 알파로 시작했다.

items.title: A ZX Spectrum Can Now Play 18 Nintendo Game & Watch Classics
items.content:
In 1982, you could climb ladders and dodge barrels on Nintendo’s pocket-sized Donkey Kong , or load a cassette into a Sinclair ZX Spectrum and play on the television. They were two very different ways to spend an afternoon. Now, thanks to a project from developer Supratim Sanyal, you can load that Game & Watch version of Donkey Kong from a tape image on the Spectrum. The same goes for 17 other Nintendo handheld games, from Oil Panic to Mario’s Cement Factory .

Sanyal released version 1.0.0 of his Game & Watch emulator on 6 November. It runs on a real 48K Spectrum and is written in assembly for the machine’s Z80 processor. The Z80 takes on the job of the Sharp SM510, the little 4-bit chip inside the supported Nintendo handhelds. The games still run their original programs. When a barrel reaches the end of a platform, or you miss a catch in Oil Panic , the rules that decide what happens next are the ones Nintendo wrote for the handheld.

From an LCD to the living-room television

Four Game & Watch games running on the ZX Spectrum 48K · SANYALnet Labs

The screen is the part I find most interesting. A Game & Watch display has a fixed set of figures and objects built into it. If Mario needs to move up a ladder, the screen switches off the segment showing him in one position and switches on the one showing him a little higher. Any given pose can only appear where the designers put it. On a television, the Spectrum has the freedom to draw Mario anywhere, but the emulator uses artwork made for the Spectrum to recreate those fixed positions. The original program still decides which figures are visible and when they change.

You can see how much Nintendo did with those constraints in Mario Bros. Anyone expecting pipes and turtles from the name is in for a surprise. The Game & Watch version puts Mario and Luigi on opposite sides of a bottling plant, where they have to keep crates moving between conveyor belts. Rain Shower uses a similarly unlikely premise, asking you to move washing out of the way of falling rain. They’re games built around watching several things at once, and the fixed displays let you read the whole situation at a glance. Stretching them out onto a television gives you a better look at how much work those little arrangements of figures were doing.

The collection spans the Wide Screen, Multi Screen and Super Color ranges. The hinged Donkey Kong is especially fun to see here. Nintendo introduced its cross-shaped directional pad on that model in June 1982, and the two screens let the action extend above the lower half of the unit. It’s easy to spot something of the DS in that open clamshell. There’s an odd bit of handheld history in seeing those two screens reproduced by a British home computer from the very same year.

Two tapes for a game that used to fit in your pocket

The download is arranged around the Spectrum’s cassette-loading routine. The first tape image contains the emulator and the graphics for the title you’ve selected. The second contains the original game program. You supply a compatible 4 KB ROM from your own collection and run the included Python utility to turn it into the second tape image. On the Spectrum, you load the first tape with LOAD "" , then switch to the second when prompted. The same TZX files also work with compatible Spectrum emulators, so the process is much the same if your Spectrum is itself running on another machine.

There’s an easier place to start. Sanyal included a new maze game called Munchy , written for the emulated Sharp chip and supplied as a complete tape. It has its own drawings and sounds, a clock and an alarm, and a faster Game B. Load the tape, use Q, A, O and P to move, and press 1 or 2 to pick a mode. There’s a small demonstration tape in the download as well, though Munchy is the one I’d point people to first. It lets you try the project without tracking down a Nintendo ROM and gives you a new game to play in the process.

items.content:
온오프라인을 가리지 않고 무분별하게 벌어지는 각종 프라이버시 침해 및 스토킹과 이에 대한 예방, 방지 및 사후 대응, 더 나아가서 개인정보 탈취 및 감시용 스파이웨어, 스토커웨어, 바이러스, 원격 조종, 추적기 등 악성코드를 통한 해킹과 스토킹 등 개인정보 침해 공격 방지와 온오프라인 프라이버시 보호를 위한 각종 다양한 지식정보를 공유하는 갤러리입니다.

매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

매니저의 부재로 인해 운영에 지장이 있다고 판단될 경우, 다른 이용자가 권한을 위임받아 마이너 갤러리를 운영할 수 있습니다.

위임 절차는 신고 게시판 > 분류 선택에 [매니저 위임]으로 위임받을 이용자가 직접 신청하면 진행됩니다. 검토 결과 운영에 적합하다고 판단되는 회원에게 매니저 권한을 위임하게 됩니다.

부매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 매니저에 의해 해임될 수 있습니다.

식별 코드 기준으로 당일 글 10개, 댓글 20개 작성 시 대왕디시콘을 3일간 사용할 수 있습니다.

즐겨찾기 폴더 추가는 즐겨찾기 on 후 우측의 폴더 아이콘을 터치하여 추가할 수 있습니다.

개별 이미지들의 위치 변경, 삭제, 별칭 추가, 폴더명 변경을 할 수 있습니다

items.title: unlocking any car from X brand in most of the world
items.content:
unlocking any car from X brand in most of the world

I've always had a soft spot for this particular car brand. Our family has owned a few of them over the years, and they've served us incredibly well. In 2023, I bought a new four wheel drive/SUV from them, and it was the first time I had access to their connected car platform.

Having looked at platforms like this before ( previous works ), I was sceptical about how secure they really were. I suspected there was something there, but life kept getting in the way of actually looking. This July, I collaborated with Sam Curry to take a look at the security of a major automaker's connected car systems. Throughout this post, I'll refer to them simply as "the automaker".

When you typically think of car hacking, it's often easy to jump into the hardware side of things, but my background sits pretty squarely in compromising internet-facing web applications and infrastructure. Regardless of all the hardware bits and bobs, it all connects back to some service that, by design, has to be reachable from the internet.

The journey started with a simple question: what infrastructure does the app talk to when I remotely unlock my car? To work this out, I downloaded the APK and decompiled it, eventually reconstructing the API requests that were being made.

Going through the code, the primary point of contact seemed to be assets under *.redacted-telematics.com.au :

dartExecutor.executeDartEntrypoint(createDefault, CollectionsKt.r(gson.toJson(new GlobalConfigParams(false, g11, com.redacted.app.xcapp.a.f69866f, "X", str)), new Gson().toJson(new ApiConfig("https://api.redacted-telematics.com.au", "https://api.redacted-telematics.com.au", "https://api.redacted-telematics.com.au" ... Almost every part of the consumer application called back to redacted-telematics.com.au . What else existed under this domain?

Running connected car infrastructure can be quite complex, and managing it requires a mix of admin tools, staging, dev, and QA environments, to make sure that customers get a clean experience. Whether all of that should be sitting on the public internet, available to anyone willing to do some basic reconnaissance, is a different story.

One asset caught my attention more than the others. admintool.redacted-telematics.com.au returned a page titled TEST HARNESS. Who can resist a subdomain with admintool in it?

Visiting this subdomain presented a very plain and grey login screen, which didn't exactly ooze quality, given it presented a logout button before we'd logged in.

I love that most single-page applications ship their entire JavaScript bundle even when all they need to render is a login page. Sure, some more modern frameworks split out JavaScript files so that they only serve what is necessary, but in this case, we could comb through the large JavaScript bundle to understand what this "admin tool" actually let you do.

Oozing quality Who even reads JavaScript bundles? Turns out this admin tool let you do quite a lot. It had a rich API that let the automaker's employees interact with customer accounts and production vehicles with very few restrictions. Reconstructing the requests, we found that a lot of these APIs needed no authentication beyond the hardcoded API keys sitting in the JavaScript bundle.

For example, we could look up user accounts by email address:

But that's just not good enough. If we want to unlock any of their cars from just knowing the number plate, we're going to need to do better than that.

In Australia, a number plate gets you the VIN (vehicle identification number) fairly easily through state-based registration lookup sites.

This isn't really a security flaw. There are plenty of legitimate reasons to want a VIN, like checking a car's true repair and insurance history before buying second-hand. If we could go from VIN to a subscriber or email, we'd complete the chain.

items.title: Miasma Worm Targets AI Coding Agents: 73 Microsoft Azure Repos Disabled
items.content:
An unprecedented supply chain attack bypasses registry-level scanners entirely, turning developer tools including Claude Code, Cursor, and Gemini CLI into execution vectors.

The Incident: On June 3, 2026, a highly sophisticated variant of the Miasma worm (also known as Mini Shai-Hulud) launched a coordinated, two-pronged attack targeting both the npm registry and developer source code repositories.

The Escalation: The attack successfully breached multiple high-profile GitHub accounts, including the official Microsoft Azure durabletask repository, using stolen Personal Access Tokens (PATs) and backdated commits to evade traditional audit trails.

The Response: In an ultra-rapid defensive maneuver, GitHub’s automated mitigation systems disabled 73 compromised repositories – including 49 directly associated with Microsoft, Azure, and Azure-Samples within a mere 105-second window .

The Vector: Instead of relying on traditional package installation hooks, Miasma targets the developer’s local environment. It abuses legitimate auto-run, hook, and rule engines within modern IDEs and AI coding assistants ( VS Code, Claude Code, Cursor, Gemini CLI ) to execute a malicious 4.3 MB staged dropper upon folder-open or agent initialization.

The Impact: Once detonated, the Bun-based worm harvests credentials for AWS, Azure, GCP, Kubernetes, npm, and GitHub, and automatically propagates by committing itself back into any repository the victim’s stolen tokens can write to.

At exactly 16:00 UTC on June 3, 2026, a silent, automated purge swept across GitHub. In a high-speed containment action lasting just 105 seconds, 73 active repositories vanished from the platform. Among them were 49 critical repositories belonging to Microsoft, Azure, and Azure-Samples.

This drastic mitigation followed alarming telemetry indicating that threat actors behind the Miasma malware family had regained write access to key cloud repositories. The compromise exploited a stolen Personal Access Token (PAT) belonging to an active Microsoft contributor.

While security firms like StepSecurity and JFrog scrambled to document an concurrent attack vector on the npm registry where 57 malicious packages were published, a second, far more insidious arm of the campaign was already silently spreading directly inside GitHub source repositories.

By bypassing registries and package managers entirely, the Miasma worm targeted the very tools developers use to write code. It didn’t wait for npm install . Instead, it waited for the developer to simply open their code editor or launch an AI coding assistant.

The genius of the Miasma repository-poisoning campaign lies in its exploit surface. When an attacker successfully pushed malicious commits to targeted codebases (such as the popular library icflorescu/mantine-datatable ), the commits added no actual code dependencies.

Instead, the attacker checked in five innocent-looking workspace configuration files and one obfuscated JavaScript file: .github/setup.js .

│ └── settings . json < - - Claude Code SessionStart Hook

│ └── setup . mdc < - - Cursor Agent Prompt Injection

│ └── settings . json < - - Gemini CLI SessionStart Hook

│ └── tasks . json < - - VS Code Automatic Folder - Open Task

├── package . json < -- Hijacked NPM Test Script

└── setup . js < - - The 4.3 MB Staged Dropper

Each of these configuration files is designed to abuse a legitimate, developer-friendly auto-run feature within popular modern tools. Opening the cloned directory in any of these environments instantly triggers execution.

Claude Code & Gemini CLI (SessionStart Hooks)

Both Anthropic’s Claude Code and Google’s Gemini CLI support custom hooks triggered when an AI agent initializes a session in a project workspace. Miasma exploits this by defining a blanket wildcard matcher that forces the agent to execute the dropper via Node.js before any developer prompt is processed.

items.title: Memory shortage spurs smartphone makers to melt used memory off old devices, then re-solder it onto new products — recycled memory to keep budget phones affordable; 'reballing' adoption to 2x by 2027.
items.content:
The smartphone industry is expected to see a spike in reballed memory adoption. According to a report by global market intelligence and research firm TrendForce, the current penetration rate is estimated at around 3–4%, with reballed memory primarily used in entry-level and budget smartphone models. However, this figure is expected to rise to 7–9% in 2027.

Reballed memory is recycled memory salvaged from older or discarded devices. The term reball comes from the process itself, in which the solder balls on a used memory chip are first melted so the chip can be removed from the old device, then re-soldered to a new device, thus allowing the component to be reused rather than discarded. You can see the process in action in the video below.

Reballing BGA Chip in 5 steps! - YouTube

This offers manufacturers a cheaper alternative to sourcing new memory chips, potentially helping them keep production costs under control. Currently, reballed 4GB LPDDR4X memory modules make up the majority of such components on the market, and they are used in 4G smartphones priced below CNY 1,299 (approximately $200).

This tactic is becoming increasingly important for smartphone makers, as customers are particularly sensitive to price increases in the budget segment. This leaves limited room to raise retail prices without affecting demand. Using reballed memory can help offset rising bill of materials (BOM) costs while allowing brands to keep entry-level devices affordable.

TrendForce expects DRAM prices to rise even further in the first quarter of 2027, which may put additional pressure on smartphone manufacturers. As a result, the use of recycled memory and other lower-specification components could gradually expand beyond the entry-level segment and into more premium smartphones. What is currently a cost-saving measure for budget devices could eventually become a broader strategy for manufacturers looking to manage expenses amid a prolonged period of high memory prices.

The rising cost of memory is also pushing PC enthusiasts and hardware hobbyists to explore unconventional ways to reuse existing DRAM chips. Recently, an electronics hobbyist converted a relatively inexpensive $120 DDR5 SO-DIMM kit into a desktop memory kit valued at around $1,000. The project involved salvaging an SK hynix 2x 16GB DDR5-5600 SODIMM kit purchased from Facebook Marketplace and reballing the chips onto custom desktop DIMM PCBs, with the resulting modules reportedly capable of reaching DDR5-7800 speeds.

Converting laptop memory into desktop DIMMs is technically demanding and requires considerable expertise and specialized equipment. Similarly, reballing memory for use in smartphones is far from straightforward, particularly given the tiny solder connections in modern BGA (Ball Grid Array) packages. Nevertheless, both developments highlight how manufacturers, repair specialists, and hardware enthusiasts are exploring alternatives to reuse existing memory to offset rising costs and limited availability.

items.title: How to Fix React State Updates with Immutable Data
items.content:
A shopping cart contains three products. A user clicks the remove button, and the application updates the array. The console confirms that the product is gone.

But the screen still shows all three items.

There is no error message. The event handler runs, and the data appears correct when inspected. Yet React doesn’t update the interface.

This is one of those bugs that can consume an afternoon because the code seems to be doing exactly what it should.

The problem usually comes down to a small but important distinction: changing an object is not the same as creating a new state value .

React treats state as a snapshot. When an object or array is stored in state, mutating its contents doesn’t automatically tell React that something changed.

Understanding this behavior helps prevent stale interfaces, makes memoization more predictable, and provides the foundation for features such as undo and redo.

1. Why React sometimes ignores state changes

const [ items , setItems ] = useState ([

< button onClick = {() => removeItem ( item . id )}>

At first glance, removeItem looks reasonable.

It finds the requested item, removes it from the array, and calls the state setter.

This method changes the existing array instead of returning a new one.

const items = [ ' A ' , ' B ' , ' C ' ];

console . log ( items === original ); // true

Although the contents changed, the array reference did not.

React compares the next state value with the current one using Object.is() .

If both values are considered equal, React can skip the update.

console . log ( Object . is ( previous , next ));

Calling setItems(items) with the same mutated array doesn’t provide React with a new state value.

currentItems.filter((item) => item.id !== id)

currentItems . filter (( item ) => item . id !== id )

filter() returns a new array containing every item except the one being removed.

React receives a different reference and can render the updated list.

There is another benefit: the original state snapshot remains unchanged.

That matters because React may still need the previous value while processing updates.

2. React compares values, not object contents

JavaScript treats primitive values and objects differently when comparing them.

Two numbers with the same value compare as equal.

Two independently created objects do not.

console . log ( Object . is ( first , second ));

Their properties are identical, but they are different objects.

Now consider two variables referencing the same object.

console . log ( Object . is ( first , second ));

Changing count doesn’t change the reference.

React doesn’t recursively inspect every property to discover whether an object has been mutated.

That would be expensive, particularly for large state structures.

Instead, state updates rely on value identity.

For objects and arrays, this means a new reference is needed when the state changes.

Create new references for the parts of state that change, and preserve existing references for the parts that don’t.

The second half is just as important as the first.

Unnecessarily creating new objects can interfere with memoization and trigger avoidable rendering work.

Arrays are among the most common sources of accidental state mutation.

Several familiar JavaScript methods modify the original array.

These include push() , pop() , shift() , unshift() , splice() , sort() , and reverse() .

They aren’t inherently bad methods. They simply need care when working with React state.

It calculates the next state from the latest state React provides, rather than relying on a potentially outdated value captured by the event handler.

Instead of finding an index and calling splice() , use filter() .

currentTodos.filter((todo) => todo.id !== id)

currentTodos . filter (( todo ) => todo . id !== id )

This also avoids a subtle bug in the original shopping cart example.

items.summary_ko: 장바구니에서 상품을 삭제했는데 화면이 바뀌지 않는 React 문제를 예로 든다. 원인은 배열이나 객체의 내용을 직접 바꾸면(mutation) React가 상태가 변경되었다고 인식하지 못하기 때문이며, 새로운 상태 값을 만들어 setter에 넘겨야 한다고 설명한다. 이 원리를 이해하면 오래된 UI를 막고, 메모이제이션을 예측 가능하게 하며, 실행 취소와 다시 실행 기능의 기반을 마련할 수 있다.
items.content_ko: 쇼핑 카트에 상품 세 개가 있고 사용자가 제거 버튼을 누르면, 콘솔에서는 배열에서 상품이 제거된 것으로 확인되지만 화면에는 여전히 세 개가 모두 보인다. 에러 메시지도 없어 원인을 찾기 어렵다. 핵심은 객체를 바꾸는 것과 새로운 상태 값을 만드는 것이 다르다는 점이다. React는 상태를 스냅샷으로 취급하므로, 상태에 든 배열이나 객체의 내용을 직접 수정해도 React는 변경이 일어났다고 판단하지 않는다. 본문은 removeItem 함수가 항목을 찾아 배열에서 제거한 뒤 setter를 호출하는 예시를 들며 이 방식의 문제를 설명하기 시작하는 대목에서 끊긴다.

items.content:
온오프라인을 가리지 않고 무분별하게 벌어지는 각종 프라이버시 침해 및 스토킹과 이에 대한 예방, 방지 및 사후 대응, 더 나아가서 개인정보 탈취 및 감시용 스파이웨어, 스토커웨어, 바이러스, 원격 조종, 추적기 등 악성코드를 통한 해킹과 스토킹 등 개인정보 침해 공격 방지와 온오프라인 프라이버시 보호를 위한 각종 다양한 지식정보를 공유하는 갤러리입니다.

매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

items.title: You should try Gleam
items.content:
If you have read my recent rant about programming languages , you'll know I've been quite interested in Gleam . Gleam is a functional language that targets BEAM, the Erlang VM, 1 with a simple syntax and interoperability with the wider BEAM ecosystem (Erlang and Elixir). Interestingly, Gleam can also target JavaScript i.e., Gleam can be compiled into JavaScript and run through Node.js.

I've been mostly using Rust for hobby projects, which at the moment is the only language that really makes coding enjoyable for me, and Gleam has managed to scratch that itch too. If you're a Rust connaisseur , then Gleam will feel familiar to you, bar a few key differences. I feel like 80% of the code I write could be copy pasted to Rust (with a tinge of search-and-replace for syntax) and it'd compile.

This post won't give an exhaustive overview of the language, if you want to learn more, I recommend the excellent interactive tour . You'll get a good feel for Gleam in under half an hour.

On its homepage, Gleam is described as "a friendly language for building type-safe systems that scale !" (emphasis theirs) which does a good job of conveying what Gleam is all about.

The syntax is extremely simple, most of the complex stuff is hidden by the Erlang runtime which you don't really have to interact with unless you want to! Of course, Gleam is a functional language, so if you have lived in a C-shaped imperative world your whole life, it might be a bit daunting at first. But if you compare it to other functional languages (OCaml, Haskell, Erlang), you'll quickly notice Gleam is much simpler. After using it a bit, it feels like all the functional parts of Rust, with a few missing ones, and none of the imperative parts.

Let's start from an example piece of code:

|> string . split ( on : "," ) // List(String)

|> list . map ( int . parse ) // List(Result(Int, Nil))

|> result . values // List(Int), the invalid entries are dropped

|> list . reduce ( fn ( acc , x ) { acc + x }) // Result(Int, Nil)

Dissecting this a bit, you can see a few specificities of Gleam:

variables in Gleam are immutable (so no mut keyword or anything like that), chained functions here all return a new element. 2 You can still shadow a binding with a new let , which is how you "update" a value.

|> (typed |> ) is the pipe operator used to chain functions on data. The main constraint is that the piped variable should be the first argument of the function in the pipe.

just like Rust, errors in Gleam are just values as part of the Result monad . 3

Comparing with the Rust code snippet, you can see that, up to a few naming choices, they look pretty similar. The main difference in this example is really the piping vs. chaining syntax. Gleam types have no methods so piping is used instead.

someOtherFunc ( param , function ( otherParam ) {

The callback must always be the last argument of the function. That is the opposite of |> , which fills the first one.

items.title: Amazon saves millions by replacing Sonnet 4.6 with Strands Decider
items.content:
For a while, Amazon and AWS teams relied on Claude Sonnet 4.6 to label tickets in an internal system

Sonnet 4.6 fit the goldilocks choice of balancing intelligence with cost. Considering it dealt with one

of the world’s largest internal ticketing systems, the nine month old model did well. However, two

Amazon engineers recently swapped out Sonnet 4.6 for

Strands Decider , a decision model we launched a month ago, that

performed just as well at 98% less cost . This change will save millions of dollars of token costs in

Carr and Mehul, who work on the internal ticketing system, walk through how this happened below.

Replacing an LLM’s job with a decision model

We had Sonnet 4.6 labeling tickets at enormous scale. The tickets could be customer escalations, capacity

requests, automated alarms, security findings, or anything else across the company that needed to fit

within 20 category types. The agent ran with a long system prompt on every ticket, generating JSON and

reasoning against a fixed set of labels.

A decision model can’t generate text. It’s first given some state and a question with a set of

options, then the decision model returns a probability for each option plus a confidence score. We saw

this method fit perfectly with ticket labeling: the state is the ticket, the options are the label

We started with the original Strands Decider 2B . On a test set of

tickets, the E4B Gemma 4 build got clearly better results, so

we switched to it. Afterwards, we tuned how confident the model needed to be before applying a label.

The results showed E4B beating production Sonnet on a separate set of our tickets.

We ran E4B on SageMaker ml.g5.xlarge instances (one A10G, 24 GB each). The model used about 19 GiB,

and one request took about 640 ms on one instance. The endpoint autoscales with traffic, but its network

was isolated, preventing outbound access to the container. SageMaker copies the model weights in from

Customers can do this too! Apart from our ticketing APIs, everything in the path is a standard AWS

service. Ticket events land in an SQS queue that then triggers a Lambda function. It reads the ticket

data and calls the model, a SageMaker AI Endpoint with Strands Decider. AppConfig holds the switch

(described below), and CloudWatch carries the logs, metrics and alarms. The stack is defined in CDK with

deployment stages for Beta, Gamma, and Prod.

Running Sonnet 4.6 and Strands Decider on the same tickets

We didn’t want to flip a switch and hope. The labeling Lambda reads a three-way setting from AWS

BEDROCK : Sonnet labels every ticket, but Strands Decider isn’t called.

DUAL : Both the Sonnet and Strands Decider models are called in parallel. The results from the

Sonnet model are applied to the ticket and compared with Strands Decider results.

DECIDER : Strands Decider labels every ticket and Bedrock isn’t called.

Claude Sonnet 4.6 Strands Decider E4B % Improvement

Average time per call 4,215 ms 897 ms 78%

Total tokens, per ticket 6,724 2,010 70%

The token drop had two sources. Strands Decider produced one output, the choice, instead of a JSON

answer. Its prompt was also much shorter than Sonnet 4.6’s. Production’s label descriptions alone are

longer than Strands Decider’s 4,096-token window, so we rewrote each of the 20 labels as a one- or

two-sentence criterion and sent them as the options of a single choice question, plus a “none” option.

items.title: I was wrong about dark mode
items.content:
They’re calling the new feature Adaptive Dark Mode ™ . I’m learning that other browsers already had a similar feature . I assumed people relied on add-ons like Dark Reader (and millions do). Regardless, pushing what is effectively an accessibility option to the forefront goes a long way to help people respect it.

My site used to have dark mode but I wasn’t happy with my colour choice and implementation. I redesigned my site back in Feb and removed it. Later I experimented with colour themes which I’ve since adapted for alternate blog banners .

Personally I prefer reading with a dark theme for long-form content. Dark is not my brand though and I don’t believe every website needs to support colour scheme preference automatically. A good browser has reader mode, I use that all the time.

What a load of rubbish. You have to understand that sometimes I just write stuff and I don’t read it back. This also contradicted my previous statement:

That said, in [current year] brands with a digital presence — all of them? — should have a colour scheme for both.

Certainly websites must work for forced dark mode. (Any site forcing light only itself upon users should go straight to jail.) So either provide a dark mode, or be prepared to test against every adaptive and forced dark mode implementation, or just let your website look broken. Probably easier to design a dark mode then?

Maybe you noticed? If not, there’s a toggle button up top. At the risk of weighing in on the conversation I’ve opted for a two-state single button. I default to system preference. The mystery button flips between light and dark. Want to return to system default? Tough luck! You shouldn’t have clicked it. Delete local storage nerd!

Technically I’m using a registered custom property with container style queries because it looks like fancy modern CSS. Three at-rules!

Most of my light/dark theming is done by customs properties. The default light colours (A) are set on the root <html> element. A style query applies the dark colours (B) on the <body> element. For edge cases that don’t follow the A/B rule I can use one of two techniques.

Either a style query inside a specific component:

Note that I set color-scheme to make light-dark() aware of the user’s choice that might override their system preference. I wonder if I can do this once:

It’s not safe to do on the root <html> element because browsers checks that for adaptive dark mode etc. I’ll stick to the verbose style queries for now until I’m sure.

There’s a sprinkle of JavaScript to use local storage for the toggle button.

It’d be better to use a cookie and a server-side template. My website is hosted on a static CDN and I’m not adding edge worker latency, so I’ll risk Flash of inAccurate coloR Theme (FART) . My site only risks a FART if a user’s choice doesn’t match their system preference. A week into my Noscript November experiment I see most websites are prone to a big FART because they rely entirely on JavaScript to enable dark mode.

I’m not happy with my button using a hidden label. Bit of a design failure I need to address later. My original goal was to have multiple themes but I ran out of time.

At the risk of soliciting replies to a question I didn’t ask, I would like your feedback on my choice of dark mode colours! Do they look nice? I don’t care whether dark mode makes your eyes bleed (turn it off) or you absolutely must have a 4-dimensional toggle.

Stephanie Eckles wrote about the same CSS technique I use. Dave Rupert has explored the light-dark() with color-scheme variations. I saw Una Kravets is using contrast-color() with style queries to do something extra fancy. Stu Robson has written in depth on dynamic colour schemes too. Sara Joy has a great CSS-Tricks article on the topic.

If you read this entire post in an RSS reader and never clicked through, what a power move!

items.title: Zero-day exploit completely defeats default Windows 11 BitLocker protections
items.content:
A zero-day exploit circulating online allows people with physical access to a Windows 11 system to bypass default BitLocker protections and gain complete access to an encrypted drive within seconds.

The exploit, named YellowKey, was published earlier this week by a researcher who goes by the alias Nightmare-Eclipse. It reliably bypasses default Windows 11 deployments of BitLocker, the full-volume encryption protection Microsoft provides to make disk contents off-limits to anyone without the decryption key, which is stored in a secured piece of hardware known as a trusted platform module (TPM). BitLocker is a mandatory protection for many organizations, including those that contract with governments.

When one disk volume manipulates another

The core of the YellowKey exploit is a custom-made FsTx folder. Online documentation of this folder is hard to find. As explained later, the directory associated with the file fstx.dll appears to involve what Microsoft calls the transactional NTFS , which allows developers to have “transactional atomicity” for file operations in transactions with a single file, multiple files, or ones that span multiple sources.

The steps for carrying out the bypass are simple:

Copy the custom FsTx folder from the Nightmare-Eclipse exploit page to an NTFS- or FAT-formatted USB drive

Connect the USB drive to the BitLocker-protected device

Boot up the device and immediately press and hold down the [Ctrl] key

There are at least two ways to accomplish the third step. One way is to boot into Windows, hold down the [Shift] key, click on the power icon, and click restart. Another is to power on the device and restart it as soon as Windows starts booting.

In either case, a command (CMD.EXE) prompt appears. The prompt has full access to the entire drive contents, allowing an attacker to copy, modify, or delete them. In a normal Windows Recovery flow, the attacker would need to enter a BitLocker recovery key. Somehow, the YellowKey exploit bypasses this safeguard. Multiple researchers, including Kevin Beaumont and Will Dormann , have confirmed the exploit works as described here.

It’s unclear what in the custom FsTx folder causes the bypass. Dormann said that it appears to be related to Transactional NTFS, which itself uses command-log file system under the hood. Dormann further noted that by looking at the Windows fstx.dll, one will see code that explicitly looks for \System Volume Information\FsTx in the FsTxFindSessions() function.”

The contents of this FsTx directory used in the YellowKey exploit reveal no strings related to RecoverySimulation.ini. It does, however, show the files and paths \??\C:\Windows\win.ini and

\??\X:\Windows\System32\winpeshl.ini, “where X:\Windows\System32\winpeshl.ini is what controls what WinRE [Windows Recovery] does when it fires up.”

Dormann, who is a senior principal vulnerability analyst at Tharros Labs, continued:

But what’s intriguing to me is: Why can the presence a \System Volume Information\FsTx directory on one volume affect the contents of ANOTHER VOLUME when it’s replayed? 🤔

In a normal WinRE session, you have a X:\Windows\System32 directory that has a winpeshl.ini file in it:

However, with the YellowKey exploit, it looks like Transactional NTFS bits on a USB Drive are able to delete the winpeshl.ini file on ANOTHER DRIVE (X:). And we get a cmd.exe prompt, with bitlocker unlocked instead of the expected Windows Recovery environment. While the TPM-only Bitlocker bypass is indeed interesting, I think the buried lede here is that a \System Volume Information\FsTx directory on one volume has the ability to modify the contents of another volume when it is replayed. To me, this in and of itself sounds like a vulnerability.

A Microsoft representative declined to answer questions sent by email about the reported vulnerability other than to say the company is investigating.

items.summary_ko: YellowKey라는 제로데이 익스플로잇이 물리적 접근으로 Windows 11의 BitLocker를 우회해 암호화된 드라이브에 접근 가능하게 한다. 수 초 내에 보호를 무효화할 수 있다.
items.content_ko: 보안 연구자 Nightmare-Eclipse가 공개한 YellowKey 제로데이 취약점은 물리적 접근만으로 Windows 11 기본 BitLocker 보호를 우회할 수 있다. BitLocker는 Microsoft가 제공하는 전체 볼륨 암호화 기술로, 신뢰할 수 있는 플랫폼 모듈(TPM)에 저장된 복호화 키 없이는 디스크 접근이 불가능하도록 설계되었다. 많은 조직과 정부 계약업체에서 필수 보호 기술로 사용 중이다. YellowKey 익스플로잇의 핵심은 커스텀으로 만들어진 FsTx 폴더 사용으로, fstx.dll과 관련된 디렉터리는 Microsoft의 transactional NTFS 기술을 활용한다.

items.title: 사생활침해 범죄가 의심 됩니다. 도움이 필요합니다
items.content:
온오프라인을 가리지 않고 무분별하게 벌어지는 각종 프라이버시 침해 및 스토킹과 이에 대한 예방, 방지 및 사후 대응, 더 나아가서 개인정보 탈취 및 감시용 스파이웨어, 스토커웨어, 바이러스, 원격 조종, 추적기 등 악성코드를 통한 해킹과 스토킹 등 개인정보 침해 공격 방지와 온오프라인 프라이버시 보호를 위한 각종 다양한 지식정보를 공유하는 갤러리입니다.

매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

매니저의 부재로 인해 운영에 지장이 있다고 판단될 경우, 다른 이용자가 권한을 위임받아 마이너 갤러리를 운영할 수 있습니다.

위임 절차는 신고 게시판 > 분류 선택에 [매니저 위임]으로 위임받을 이용자가 직접 신청하면 진행됩니다. 검토 결과 운영에 적합하다고 판단되는 회원에게 매니저 권한을 위임하게 됩니다.

부매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 매니저에 의해 해임될 수 있습니다.

식별 코드 기준으로 당일 글 10개, 댓글 20개 작성 시 대왕디시콘을 3일간 사용할 수 있습니다.

즐겨찾기 폴더 추가는 즐겨찾기 on 후 우측의 폴더 아이콘을 터치하여 추가할 수 있습니다.
